full_judgment:
Md. Muzammel Hossain, CJ: I have gone through the judgments delivered by Surendra Kumar Sinha, J and Nazmun Ara Sultana, J. I agree with the judgment of Nazmun Ara Sultana, J.

SK Sinha, J : I have had the advantage of reading the draft copy of the judgment pre-pared by Nazmun Ara Sultana, J I agree with the conclusion she has reached but I wish, however, to add my opinion in support of the conclusion she has arrived at. The points to be decided in these appeals are: (1) if a director of a Bank Companies Act, 1991 is removed from the Board on a ground other than the grounds on which show cause notice was issued and if such removal is made without affording him a personal hearing whether such removal violates the principles of natural justice and (2) if there is breach of the principles of fairness in taking such action, was such breach is curable by the appellate process provided in section 48 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 (Act of 1991).

3. Short facts relevant for the disposal of these points are that while performing as directors of the Social Investment Bank Ltd., the appellants were served with show cause notices alleging that (1) while in the Board of Directors of the Social Investment Bank Ltd., they acquired shares of M/s. Homeland footwear Ltd., a defaulter company in payment of loans taken from Social Investment Bank Ltd, Rupali Bank Ltd. and Al-Arafah Islami Bank Ltd. during the period from 13th March, 1997 to 24th February, 1998 and became the directors of the Board, (2) they concealed the fact of their involvement with a defaulter company to the Social Investment Bank Ltd., (3) no permission as required under section 27 of Act of 1991 was taken from of the said three bank companies while they resigned from the Board of Homeland Footwear Ltd., and (4) such involvement was detrimental to the public interest as well as detrimental to the interest of depositors of Social Investment Bank Ltd.

4. Appellants submitted replies to the show cause notices on 29th October, 2001 through their Lawyer. Thereupon, the Bangladesh Bank by its order under memo dated 13th July, 2002 removed the appellants from the Board on the grounds, inter alia, that (1) they concealed from the Bangladesh Bank in their returns the fact availing of loans of their concern M/s Homeland Footwear Ltd., (2) they influenced the Social Investment Bank Ltd. in not impleading them in the suit instituted for recovery of outstanding loan, and (3) they influenced the Social Investment Bank Ltd. in not invoking section 17 Act of 2001, which acts were contrary to the interest of the depositors. Appellants, thereupon, preferred appeals from the orders of removal before the Board of Directors of the Bangladesh Bank. The Board of Directors, as it appears from the orders, considered the pros and cons of the matter and afforded them personal hearing as desired and then rejected the appeals is on 24th April, 2003 and communicated the said orders to them on 26th April, 2003. The appellants, thereupon, prayed for judicial review of the said orders of the appellate authority in the High Court Division.

5. Section 17 of Act, 2001 provides for the vacation of the office of a director. It states that (ka) if a director of a bank company or the bank company fails to repay the loan or installments taken from any other financial organisation, or (kha) if a director of bank company fails to pay any amount of loan to which he was a guarantor, or (ga) such director undertakes any responsibility of loan by writing and fails to repay the amount of a loan even after receipt of notice for payment within two months, the office of director shall cease vacant on the expiry of the period. Sub-sections (2), (3), (4) and (5) of section 17 provide for the procedure for taking legal action against the director or bank company by the Bangladesh Bank and for recovery of the money.

6. Section 46 of the Act of 1991 empowers the Bangladesh Bank to remove the chairman, director or chief executive of a Bank Company, if it is satisfied that it is necessary for the public interest or to prevent the affairs of a bank company from acting detrimental to the interest of its depositors or for ensuring the proper management of a bank company for reason to be recorded in writing subject to the condition that before making such an order, the person against whom the order is made shall be given a reasonable opportunity to explain his position against the proposed action. Under this provision the Bangladesh Bank has been given wider discretionary power to remove such person from the date of issuance of notice pending consideration of the explanation if it is satisfied that in case of delay in removing him, it would be prejudicial to the public interest or affect the interest of the bank company or its depositors. It is provided in section 48(1) that the Governor of the Bangladesh Bank shall not make any order under section 46 unless he is satisfied on a report of the standing committee set up by the Bank. It is provided in sub-section (2) of section 48 that any person aggrieved by such order may prefer an appeal to the Board of Directors of the Bangladesh Bank, whose decision shall be final, and the action taken as above shall not be called in question before any Court or tribunal or any other authority.

7. It was urged on behalf of the appellants in the High Court Division that the Bangladesh Bank issued the Orders of removal relying upon the inquiry report of the standing committee. In the alternative, it was pointed out that the recommendation of the standing committee was reflected in the orders of removal and that there was no independent application of mind in taking the decision. The High Court Division found no force in the contentions that no independent opinion was formed by the authority before making the orders of removal.

8. The High Court Division held that the appellants did not take any step for rectification of the returns submitted before the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies even after disclosure of that fact in the show course notices; that if they had no interest in M/s Homeland Footwear Ltd. they could have taken steps for rectification; that as Title Suit No. 138 of 2003 was instituted two years after the order of removal in which Bangladesh Bank was not made party, the decree passed in that suit was not binding upon the Bangladesh Bank; that the Bangladesh Bank considered the report of the standing committee before making the order under section 46 of the Act but the appellants did not make any statement about the standing committee's report in the writ petitions; that the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the writ respondent Nos. 1 and 2 is accompanied by a copy of the inspection report and the inspection was made by responsible officers of the Bangladesh Bank, and the committee after consideration of all documents relating to Homeland Footwear Ltd. came to the conclusion that the appellants were directors of that defaulter company and even after their resignation, those posts were replaced by their close relations such as wife, daughter etc.; that there are sufficient materials before the authority in removing the appellants from the Board and that the Bangladesh Bank removed the appellants in accordance with law.

9. Leave was granted to consider four points namely; (1) the orders of removal were violative of the principles of natural justice, inasmuch as, the appellants were not given personal hearing, (2) the appellants particularly Kamal Uddin Ahmed, the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 9 of 2004 having not been appointed as Director of Homeland Footwear Ltd. at the Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the Company or in the alternative, without his consent in accordance with sections 91 and 93 of the Companies Act, 1994, (Act of 1994), the question of concealment of fact to the Bangladesh Bank does not arise at all, (3) in view of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 138 of 2003 against the Homeland Footwear Ltd. declaring that the appellants are not directors of the Company and that the returns in form XII purported to have been submitted with the Register, Joint Stock Companies were without compliance of the provisions of the Companies Act, such as, without any election in any meetings of the company, and (4) the disposal of the appeals by the Board of Directors of the Bangladesh Bank was unlawful and without jurisdiction, inasmuch as, those appeals were-disposed of during the pendency of the suit.

10. The question is whether the orders of removal were made on grounds other than those mentioned in the show cause notices. We noticed that the substance of the show cause notices was that the appellants suppressed/ concealed material facts of becoming share-holders-directors of M/s Homeland Footwear Ltd, a defaulter company, with three banks particularly to social Investment Bank Ltd, and resigned as directors of the defaulter company without taking prior approval of the Board of Directors of the borrowing banks in violation of section 27A of the Act of 1991, which acts are detrimental to the interest of the depositors. In the orders of removal, it had been pointed out that the appellants concealed the facts of availing loan benefits of their concern M/s Homeland Footwear Ltd. to the Bangladesh Bank, for which, Bangladesh Bank could not invoke powers provided in section 17 of the Act of 2001, which act is contrary to the interest of the depositors of the bank. The substance of show cause notices and the orders of removal are concealment of facts by the appellants and that such concealment of facts are decremented to the interest of the depositors. Therefore, it cannot be said that they were removed on different grounds.

11. As regards the violation of the principles of natural justice, admittedly the appellants were afforded opportunities to explain their position before the orders of removal were made. Even in the said orders, it was clearly pointed out that the appellants had the right to prefer appeals under section 48(2) of Act of 1991, if they were at all aggrieved by the orders. In their replies to the show cause notices, the appellants did not express their desire of giving them any personal hearing. On the concluding paragraph 13, it was stated "should you need any clarification or further assistance in resolving the issue, our client is ready to extend all co-operation and would not hesitate to attend any hearing". This statement is self explanatory that the appellants did not claim any personal hearing. What they stated was that if the Bangladesh Bank required any clarification from them in resolving the issues, they could appear in person at the hearing. It was only when the materials before the Bank were not sufficient and if the appellate authority required their presence for any clarification; the Bangladesh Bank would be at liberty to ask them to appear at the hearing. In the alternative it may be inferred that the appellants left the matter to the discretion of the Bangladesh Bank to consider whether or not the materials placed before it were sufficient to dispose of the appeals.

12. Even if it is assumed that the Bangladesh Bank ought to have heard the appellants in person before taking actions against them, the question is whether the decision vitiated by the breach of the principles of fair hearing. The disposal of this issue requires the examination of the relevant provisions of the Act of 2001. Section 46(2) of Act, 1991 mandated that the Bangladesh Bank has an obligation to give an opportunity to make a representation by the person proposed to be proceeded against the disciplinary action, which is a right given to such person and nothing more is provided in law. The Bangladesh Bank had no discretion as regards the issuance of show cause notice before removal of a director but it was not obligatory on its part for affording them any personal hearing. If the appellants had expressed their desire of a personal hearing and if the decisions were taken ignoring such prayer, they could have raised a plea for breach of fairness in taking the decisions i.e. by failure to allow them an opportunity to be heard.

13. This breach could be raised from two legal sources; statutory constructions and legitimate expectation. As to the statutory constructions, law does not provide as such. There is no provision for an oral hearing to be made by the Act of 2001 and the requirement of fairness does not arise unless they can show prejudice which they failed to substantiate. They had a right in law to an oral hearing which was never asserted by them until they filed appeal before the Board. As regards the legitimate expectation, there must be foundation in support of it. The doctrine of legitimate expectation in essence imposes a duty to act fairly. Whether the expectation is reasonable or legitimate in the context is a question of fact in each case. A bonafide decision of the public authority would satisfy the requirement of non-arbitratiness and withstand judicial scrutiny. Every such expectation does not by itself fructify into a right and therefore, it does not amount to a right in the conventional sense.

14. The concept of natural justice is not codified canons and this concept has been developed by judicial pronouncements. The first rule was stated in Earl of Derby's case, (1605) 12 Co. Rep 114 is 'memo judex in causa sua or nemo debet esse judex in propria sua', that is, no man shall be a judge of his own cause. This principle is a great humanising principle intented to invest law with fairness and to secure justice and over the years it has grown into a widely pervasive rule affecting large areas of administrative action. The second rule is 'andi alteram partern', that is, no man should be condemned unheard.

15. If we look at the genesis of the expression "natural justice' we find that Lord Esher MR in Voinet vs Barrett, (1885) 55 Li QB 39 explained the meaning of 'natural justice' that is "the natural sense what is right and wrong'. The expression was used in the past inter-changeably with the expressions 'natural law' 'natural equity' eternal law' the laws of god'.

In the leading case of RV Chancellor of Cambridge, (1723) Fortescue 202, known as Dr. Bentley's case, the expression 'natural justice' was used in the pleadings and the expression 'law of nature' in the note of the judgment in relation to the same principle. Sir Henry Maine in International Law, Lecture 11 says:

"Seen in the light of stoical doctrine the Law of Nations came to be identified with the Law of Nature; that is to say, with a number of supposed principles of conduct which man in society obeys simply because he is a man. Thus the Law of Nature is simply the Law of Nations seen in the light of a peculiar theory. A passage in Roman Institutes shows that the expressions were practically convertible" and again: "The Law of Nations so far as it is founded on the principles of Natural Law is equally binding in every age and upon all mankind".

16. It is that the medieval civil and canon lawyers relied on a conception of natural law and, when confronted with a case for which there was no precedent or upon which their law was silent, purported to resort to the Law of Nature which they deemed to be fundamental to all law. In effect it appears that what they were doing was to make up their own minds as to what was fair, just and beneficial to all concerned. When common Law of England was being developed, a similar process was invoked by the common law courts, and a divine origin was frequently ascribed to natural law.

17. In 1760 in the famous case of Moses vs Macferlan, (1760) 2 Barr. 1005, which was described by Lord Mansfield as 'an equitable action to recover back money which ought not in justice to be kept' the Chief Justice said:

"In one word, the gist of this kind of action is that the defendant, upon the circumstances of the case, is obliged by the ties of natural justice and equity to refund the money."

18. Here the expression 'natural Justice' was not clearly used in its restricted modem sense but was synonymous with natural law; in the same way as the expression 'equity' did not refer to technical equity i.e. the equity of the Chancery Court, but to jus natural. In other words 'natural justice' and 'equity' in this passage meant the same thing i.e. natural law. On a historical survey of the above opinions we find that:

a) the doctrine of the supremacy and imputability of natural law was once held to be part of the law of England;

b) in the same way as the Romans identified jus natural with their jus gentium so the English judges identified natural law with the common law of England; and

c) natural justice is part of natural law and of the common law.

19. On the strength of the above opinions, particularly of Dr. Bentleys case, it was argued many a times with confidence that not only is natural justice part of natural law but it is that part of natural law which relates to the administration of justice. In due course of time the courts have devised a kind of code of fair administrative procedure. Natural justice plays much the same part in British law as does 'due process of law' in the Constitution of the united states. The principle has a very wide general application in the numerous areas discretionary administrative power. As the administrative powers continually grow more drastic, it is only by procedural fairness that they are rendered tolerable.

20. This doctrine did not survive far into the nineteenth century. The fact remains that the supremacy of Parliament ultimately became a fundamental principle of the British Constitution, and in 1842, it was possible for the judicial committee of the privy council in Lagan vs Burslem, (1842) 4 Moore PC 284, 296, to observe:

"As to what has been said of an Act of Parliament not binding if it is contrary to reason that can receive no countenance from any court of justice whatever. A Court of justice cannot set itself above the legislature."

21. In 1871 the Court of common pleas in Lee vs Bude & Torrington Junction Railway Co., (1871; LR 6 PC 576, Willes, J went further saying;

"It was once said - I think in Hobart that if an Act of Parliament were to create a man judge in his own cause, the Court might disregard it. That dictum, however, stands as a warning, rather than an authority to be followed. We sit here as servants of the Queen and the legislature. Are we to act as regents over what is done by Parliament with the consent of the Queen, lords and commons? I deny that any such authority exists. If an Act of Parliament has been obtained improperly, it is for the legislature to correct it by repealing it; but so long as it exists as law, the courts are bound to obey it. The proceedings here are judicial, not autocratic, which they would be if we could make laws instead of administering them."

22. These expressions came from the principle which is known to all 'audi alteram partem' i.e. no one should be condemned unheard. In this connection it is pertinent to quote an observation of the Lord Chancellor Earl of Selborne in Arthur John Spackman vs Phimstead District Board of Works, (1885) 10 AC 299:

"No doubt, in the absence of special provisions as to how the person who is to decide is to proceed, law will imply no more than that the substantial requirements of justice shall not be violated. He is not a judge in the proper sense of the word; but he must give the parties an opportunity of being heard before him and stating their case and their view. He must give notice when he will proceed with the matter and he must act honestly and impartially and not under the dictation of some other person or persons to whom the authority is not given by law. There must be no malversation of any king. There would be no decision within the meaning of the statute if there were anything of that sort done contrary to the essence of justice".

23. Mr. Abdur Razzak, learned counsel has cited the case of Canara Bank, vs Debasis Das, (2003) 4 SCC 557, in which, Arijit Pasayat, J. echoed the above views observing:

"Concept of natural justice has under-gone a great deal of change in recent years. Rules of natural justice are not rules embodied always expressly in a statute or in rules framed thereunder. They may be implied from the nature of the duty to be performed under a statute. What particular rule of natural justice should be implied and what its context should be in a given case must depend to a great extent on the facts and circumstances of that case, the framework of the statute under which the enquiry is held. The old distinction between a judicial act and an administrative act has withered away. Even an administrative order which involves civil consequences must be consistent with the rules of natural justice.

24. What we really find from the above arguments is that a person should not be condemned without giving him an opportunity of being heard before the action is taken against him. It varies from fact to fact the extent of giving such opportunity are not uniform for all contractual domestic tribunals. There is, however, divergence of opinion in this regard; the latest view expressed was Stranghton, LJ in R. Ealing Magistrates Court, ex P Fammaran (1996) 8 Adamn LR 351 'holding there must be demonstrable beyond doubt' that the result would have been otherwise'. In this regard Mr. Mahmudul Islam has referred to a passage from Wade's Administrative Law, 5th Edition, Page 526, thus: while futile writs may not be issued, a distinction has to be made according to the nature of the decision. Thus, in relation to cases other than those relating to admitted or indisputable facts, there is a considerable divergence of opinion whether the applicant can be compelled to prove that the outcome will be in his favour or he has to prove a case of substance or if he can prove a 'real likelihood of success of if he is entitled to relief even if there is some remote chance of success. We may, however, point out that even in cases where the facts are not all admitted or beyond dispute, there is a considerable unanimity that the courts can, in exercise of their 'discretion' refuse certiorai, prohibition, mandamus, or injunction even though natural justice is not followed."

25. In State Bank of Patiala vs SK Sharma, (1996) 3 SCC 364, it was observed that even in relation to statutory provision requiring notice, a distinction is to be made between cases where the provision is intended for individual benefit and where a provision is intended to protect public interest. In the former case, it can be waived while in the latter case, it cannot be waived. In the cases, in hand, even the appellants did not dispute that the minimum requirement of the statutory provisions of law has not been followed. In the concise statement of the respondent Nos.  5-8, it is stated that the Bangladesh Bank appointed a high power inspection committee to inquire into the matter and found the allegations to be true. Thereafter, the matter was sent to the standing committee under section 48 of Act, 2001, which recommended the removal of the appellants. The Bangladesh Bank upon perusal of the same satisfied that in the event of taking no legal action, public interest would be hampered and then issued the show cause notices. The appellants made representations in reply to the notices issued upon them. In view of the above, it can be inferred that there is no breach to the principle and no failure of justice or any prejudice has seemed to have been occasioned in the matter. The action having been taken for the public interest after exhausting the procedures provided in the Act of 1991, it can be said that there was no breach of the principle.

26. Learned Counsel for the appellants tried to impress this Division that the orders of removal having been made without affording personal hearing to the appellants there was violation of the principle. Reference was given to the case of Bangladesh Telecom (Pvt) Ltd. Vs. T&T Board, 48 DLR (AD) 20 in support of the contention. In the petition of appeal made under section 48 of Act of 1991, the appellant Kamal Uddin Ahmed expressed his desire for personal hearing along with his lawyer. In the impugned order it was pointed out by the Bangladesh Bank that “আপনার আবেদনের প্রেক্ষিতে পর্ষদ সভায় আপনার ব্যক্তিগত শুনানী ও গ্রহন করা হইল।” Admittedly, this appellant was heard in person before making the impugned order.

<u>27. As noticed above section 46(1) does not provide for a personal hearing of the person against whom the order of removal will be made. Sub-section (2) of section 46 ordains that 'reasonable opportunity' shall be given before an order under sub-section (1) is made for explaining position against the proposed order. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, contended that the point as to personal hearing merits no consideration on two grounds, firstly, even if it is assumed that the personal hearing ought to have been given to the appellants before making of the orders of removal, the defect was cured by reason of affording them personal hearing by the appellate authority, and secondly, the ground for removal was made for suppression of the material facts, on which ground show cause notices were issued stating that this suppression affected the interest of the share holders of the Bank, and therefore, there was no violation of natural justice. Reliance was given to the case of Lloyd vs MC Mohon, (1987) AC 625.</u>

28. In T&T case referred to by the learned counsel, the writ petitioner entered into an agreement with T&T Board permitting it to install and operate four types of communication system in the private sector specifying the items to be operated upon. There was a clause authorizing the writ petitioner to transfer a portion of the licencing right for joint venture purpose provided it obtains prior written permission from T&T Board. Pursuant thereto, T&T Board issued licence and permitted to operate and maintain the communication system. Writ petitioner alleged that it entered into a joint venture agreement, spent huge money towards the construction of exchange building, imported equipment for cellular radio telephone and while it was performing its responsibility as per agreement, T&T Board issued show cause notice to exclude cellular radio telephone system from the agreement by way of amendment stating that the writ petitioner established cellular radio telephone system and made it operational by the joint venture company without prior written permission of T&T Board and also without transferring its licence to the joint venture company. In the context of the matter, this Division held that the cancellation letter in respect of the agreement was in effect a revocation of the licence; that a licence is a privilege created in favour of the licencee and unless the statute excludes the operation of the principle of natural justice, a show cause notice is a must for revocation of the licence. This case is quite distinguishable and not applicable in this case. Further in these cases, proper show cause notices were issued upon the appellants before taking action against them and in the appellate forum, the appellant Kamal Uddin was afforded a personal hearing.

29. Wade in his Administrative law, Ninth Edn, page 527 stated, natural justice does not require that there should be a right of appeal from any decision. This is an inevitable corollary of the fact that there is no right of appeal against a statutory authority unless statute so provides. Whether a hearing given on appeal is an acceptable substitute for a hearing not given, or not properly given, before the initial decision is in some cases an arguable question. In principle there ought to be an observance of natural justice equally at both stages; and accordingly natural justice is violated if the true change is put forward only at the appeal stage. If natural justice is violated at the first stage, the right of appeal is not so much a true right of appeal as a corrected initial hearing; instead of a fair trial followed by appeal, the procedure is reduced to unfair trial followed by fair trial.

30. Megarry, J. in Leary vs National Union of vehicle Builders (1971) Ch. 34 held in a trade union expulsion case that as a general rule, a failure of natural justice in the trial body cannot be cured by a sufficiency of natural justice in the appellate body. He distinguished a Canadian case in which a law student had been refused leave to take a degree; he had been allowed to submit only a written statement to the faculty council, but on appeal he had been given a full oral hearing and represented by counsel. The Supreme Court of Canada held that the appeal cured any earlier defect (King vs University of Saskatchewan (1969) 6 DLR (3rd) 120). 'In New Zealand, also, in Reid vs Rowley (1977) 2 N2LR 472, it has been held that a fair appeal does not normally redeem a failure of natural justice at first instance, though it may be taken into account in considering the award of discretionary remedies.

31. In Calvin vs Carr (1980) A.C. 574 approving the judgment of Cooke, J. in Reid vs Rowley, Megarry, J. observed, 'general rule' was too broadly stated, since in some cases members of orgaisation, whose rights depend upon contract, 'should be taken to have agreed to accept what in the end is a fair decision, notwithstanding some initial defect'. An appeal to the committee, it is said, of the Australian Jockey club was held, of this reason, to cure an initial decision of the stewards, which failed to observe the principles of natural justice in disqualifying the owner of the horse found to have been raced improperly.

32. In the case of a public authority acting under statutory powers it would seem paradoxical to interpret the provision of a right of appeal as meaning that the initial decision may be less fair than it would have to be if not subject to appeal. In Ridge vs Baldwin, (1964) A.C. 40, the House of Lords did not allow the chief constable's unsuccessful administrative appeal to the Home Secretary to prejudice his right to a fair hearing before the watch committee. In Rechromex Nickel Mines Ltd. (1970) 16 DLR (3rd) 273, it was held that an appeal may have greater effect where the appeal tribunal, has original as well as appellate jurisdiction.

33. The House of Lords in the case of Lloyd vs MC Mahon, (1987) AC 625, answered the point exhaustively. Issues raised in that appeal was (1) is an auditor, in carrying out an audit under section 20 of the Local Government Finance Act, 1982 obliged to offer any person who is likely to be adversely affected by the audit an oral hearing because (i) on a proper construction of the statutory provision such a duty is to be imported or (ii) such a duty arises from a legitimate expectation? (2) If submission of point 1 (one) is wrong, and the auditor has a discretion whether to offer a person who is likely to be adversely affected by the audit an oral hearing, should such an opportunity, in fairness, have been given to the appellants councilors by the district auditor? (3) If the district auditor was in breach of the principles of fairness, was such breach curable by the appellate process under section 20(3) of the Act of 1982, and if so, was it so cured by the appeal to the Divisional Court?

34. It was argued by Lawton LJ, the proceeding before the appellate authority was "truly a rehearing and not, as Mr. Blom Cooper suggested, a critical examination of a reasoned decision. In my judgment the appellants, and each of them, had a fair and adequate opportunity of dealing with any findings and comments which were critical of or adverse to them in the district auditor's written reasons dated 6th September, 1985. Such unfairness as there was in the way he performed his duties was cured by the appeal." Dillon L.J. following the case of Calvin V Carr (1980) A.C. 514 and another case, 12 ALR 379, argued "I have no doubt that in the present case, if there was any failure of fairness on the part of the district auditor, either in not offering the appellants an oral hearing or not offering them an opportunity to comment on his proposed findings before he rejected the appellants' representations as untrue, that failure was fully cured by the hearing in the Divisional Court under the statutory appeal process". Woolf L.J. in his separate opinion concurred with the above arguments stating "accordingly I have come to the conclusion that when the proceedings including the hearing before the Divisional Court, are considered as a whole the allegation of unfairness is not made out".

35. Lord Keith of Kinkel in his separate opinion argued "Upon the view which I take, that the district auditor's decision was not vitiated by procedural unfairness, the question whether such unfairness, had it existed, was capable of being cured by the appeal to the High Court does not arise directly for decision. It is, however, my opinion that the particular appeal mechanism provided for by section 20(3) of the Act of 1982, considered in its con-text, is apt to enable the court, notwithstanding that it finds some procedural defect in the conduct of an audit which has resulted in a certificate based on willful misconduct, to inquire into the merits of the case and arrive at its own. decision thereon. Section 20(3)(b) empowers the court to "confirm the decision or quash it and give any certificate which the auditor could have given".

36. Lord Bridge of Harwich in his separate opinion stated that rules of natural justice are not engraved on tablets of stone. To use "the phrase which better expresses the underlying concept, what the requirements of fairness demand when anybody, domestic, administrative or judicial, has to make a decision which will affect the rights of individuals depends on the character of the decision making body, the kind of decision it has to make and the statutory or other framework in which it operates. In particular, it is well established that when a statute has conferred on anybody the power to make decisions affecting individuals, the Courts will not only require the procedure prescribed by the statute to be followed but will readily imply so much and no more to be introduced by way of additional procedural safe-guards as will ensure the attainment of failurness." His Lordship then examined the Act of 1982 and some decisions particularly Calvin vs Carr (1980) A.C. 574 and posed a query such as, 'The question how far in domestic and administrative two-tier adjudicatory systems a procedural failure at the level of the first-tier can be remedied at the level of the second tier..." and concluded the argument thus: "But I am clearly of opinion that when the Court has, as here, in fact conducted a full hearing on the merits and reached a conclusion that the issue of a certificate was justified, it would be an erroneous exercise of discretion nevertheless to quash the certificate on the ground that, before the matter reached the court, there had been some defect in the procedure followed." Other three Lord Justices concurred with the above opinion.

37. Mr. Abdur Razzaq has also referred to the case of Calvin vs Carr, (1979) 2 All ER 440. As observed above, this case was considered in MC Mahon. In that case, it was held that there was no absolute rule that defects in natural justice at an original hearing could or could not be cured by appeal proceedings which had been correctly and fairly conducted. However, where a person had joined an organisation or body and was deemed, on the rules of that organisation and the contractual context in which he joined, to have agreed to accept with at in the end was a fair decision, notwithstanding some initial defect, the task of the courts was to decide, in the light of the agreements made and having regard to the course of the proceedings, whether at the end of those proceedings there had been a fair result reached by fair methods. On the facts, those who took part in racing were deemed to have accepted the Rules of Racing and to be bound by the decisions of bodies set up under the rules, provided they received fair treatment and a consideration of their case on its merits.

38. The views taken in MC Mahon have been approved in latter cases in England as well as the Supreme Court of India. In Debasis Das case, (2003) 4 SCC 557, referred to by Mr. Razzak, Canara Bank, a government undertaking issued four charge sheets against Debasis Das. In pursuance of an enquiry report relating to one charge-sheet, the disciplinary authority passed an order of dismissal. The authority reinstated him pursuant to a judgment of Calcutta High Court and thereafter, he was issued with three office orders to proceed with inquiries relating to other three charge-sheets. The employee took the stand that he was exonerated from the charges and the proceedings had been dropped. The inquiry officer conducted the enquiry in presence of the employee, and submitted a report. The disciplinary authority sent copy of the enquiry report to the employee and asked for his reply. Ultimately the disciplinary authority found the employee guilty of the charges. It was pointed out on behalf of the employee that though the enquiry officer permitted the employee to file written briefs after  written briefs were submitted by the presiding officer, the employee had not received copy of written briefs, there was violation of natural justice as the inquiry officer did not consider his written briefs before the recommendation was made. The second point raised on behalf of the employee is that merely because the appellate authority granted opportunity of personal hearing, that did not cure the incurable defect in the proceedings. In that case the Canara Bank Officers Employees' (Conduct) Regulation, 1976, particularly Regulation 6(18) which was relevant to resolve the controversy came into consideration, which provided that the enquiry authority may, after completion of production of evidence hear the presiding officer and the employee or permit them to file written briefs of the respective cases.

39. In the facts of the given case, it was observed that the written briefs are relatable to the case of the party concerned otherwise. The expression 'respective case' could be meaning-less, that in the 'appeal before the Appellate Authority findings of the inquiry officer were challenged and, therefore, the question of any prejudice does not arise since the employee had the opportunity to meet the stand of the Bank, it was to his advantage, and opportunity for personal hearing was also granted, though Regulation 6(18) does not even speak of granting such an opportunity." The Supreme Court accepted the arguments on behalf of the Canara Bank observing that 'unless failure of justice is occasioned or that it would not be in public interest to dismiss a petition on the fact situation of a case, this court may refuse to exercise the said jurisdiction.... Personal hearing was granted by the Appellate Authority, though not statutorily prescribed. In a given case post-decisional hearing can obliterate the procedural deficiency of a predecisional hearing.'

40. In King vs University of Saskatchewan, (1969) SCR 678, Spence, J speaking for the majority argued:

"Any possible failure of natural justice before the special appeal committee, the executive committee, or the full faculty council is quite unimportant when the senate, the appeal body under the provisions of the University Act and also the body in control of the granting of degrees has exercised its function with no failure to accord natural justice. If there were any absence of natural justice in the inferior tribunals, it was cured by the presence of such natural  justice before the senate appeal committee."

41. The above views have been approved in a latter case by the Supreme Court of Canada by majority in Harelkin vs University of Regina, (1979) 2 SCR 561. Beetz J speaking for the majority observed 'I accordingly find it impossible to distinguish king from Denton and Leary (1969) N2LR 256, (1970) 3 WLR 434 (Ch.D) on the question whether the failure to observe natural justice can be cured in appeal.  " In that case, the appellant, a student under the University of Regina was required by the University authorities to discontinue his studies. The University Act, 1974 provided an appeal to a committee of the University Council, obliged to 'hear and decide'. The committee heard one side the University and decided adversely to the student. The student did not know what was placed against him in the committee nor was he afforded an opportunity to correct or contradict any statement prejudicial to his position. His request for rehearing was also refused by the authority. He then instituted a petition for certiorari and mandamus for quashing the order. It was contended on the part of the University that the student was not damnified because he had a further appeal to a committee of the Senate of the University also charged with the duty, on appeal, to hear and decide. The trial Judge rejected the contentions of the University to hold a hearing pursuant to section 78(1)(c) of the Act of 1974 and to allow the student to be present to be heard to present evidence and to be represented by counsel, with respect to the refusal of the authority to allow him to pursue higher studies. The Court of appeal reversed holding that 'where there is a right of appeal certiorari should not be granted except under special circumstances'. On appeal from the said decision, Beetz, J. while maintaining the Court of appeal observed:

"This may be so, but it is of little importance where the superior appellate jurisdiction is equipped with the means to remedy all injustices. I have reached the conclusion that appellant's right of appeal to the senate committee provided him with an adequate alternative remedy. In addition, this remedy was in my opinion a more convenient remedy for appellant as well as for the University in terms of costs and expeditiousness.

42. The above views were taken with approval by Sabyasachi Mukherji, CJ in Charam Lal Sahu vs Union of India, AIR 1990 SC 1480. In that case the constitutionality of the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985 was challenged. It was claimed that the rights of the victims to fight for their own cases and to assert their own grievances have kept away. Sections 3, 4, and 11 of the Act are violative of Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution. It was claimed on behalf of the state that the Act enabled the victims to exercise their rights of participation in the proceedings and as they had notice of the incident and the pendency of proceeding, no notice was required to be served upon them either under the constitutional requirements or under the general principles of natural justice. It has been held: "If the statute conferring the power is silent with regard to the giving of a predecisional hearing to the person affected the administrative decision after post decisional hearing was good."

43. Now turning to the other point raised at the Bar, every company is required to keep at its registered office a Register of its directors, managers and managing agents containing the particulars including their holding directorship, if any, and shall submit return to the Registrar in prescribed form (form XII) which shall contain the particulars as mentioned above in accordance with the procedures prescribed by section 115 of the Companies Act. It has been found by the Bangladesh Bank in course of inquiry that the Homeland Footwear Ltd. submitted returns on 9th April, 1997 and 25th January, 1990 before the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies. The allegation against the appellants are that they purchased shares of Homeland Footwear Ltd. and became directors of that company which is a defaulter company with Social Investment Bank Ltd. and two other banks and that the appellants kept concealed of the said fact.

44. There are two modes for appointment of a Director of a private Company. The subscribers of the memorandum shall be deemed to be the directors of a company as per clause (a) to section 91(1) of the Act of 1994, The other manner of appointment is by way of election in the Annual General Meeting (AGM). And the other mode is the filling up of the casual vacancy on the retirement of a director. The appellants not being the subscribers of the company, the first clause is not applicable to them. The positive case of the Bangladesh Bank is that the appellants acquired shares and then became directors of the company, therefore, clause (c) to section 91(1) of Act, 1994 is attracted in their case. So, election by the, members in AGM as contended by the learned counsel for the appellants is not necessary for them for such appointment. The Board has power to appoint a director and this power might be exercised notwithstanding that the strength of the Board had fallen below the minimum required and below the quorums prescribed by the articles. They filled up the casual vacancy of the Board of the defaulter company in accordance with law. Further, returns in form XII are required to be submitted by the company, which are kept with the office of Registrar, Joint Stock Companies which are public documents. There is presumption in favour of official acts being legal until contrary is proved. The official acts are presumed to be legally performed and where the jurisdiction of an officer is not questioned in the Court, it must be presumed that he acted within the jurisdiction. Therefore, this point merits no consideration.

45. Next point is the decree passed in TS No. 138 of 2003, in which, it was declared that the appellants were not the directors of M/s Footwear Ltd. that returns in form XII were illegal and that the Registrar was directed to rectify the record deleting their names. Now the question is whether these declarations contravened the decision of the Bangladesh Bank. Mr. Rokunuddin Mahmud argued that the appeals having been disposed of after the decree of the civil court, such orders have no legal basis at all.

46. The show cause notices upon the appellants were issued on 8th October, 2001 disclosing that while the directors of Social Investments Bank Ltd., they became directors of a company which was defaulter with three Banks and concealed that fact to the creditor banks. It is stated in paragraph 2(XIV) of the respondents concise statement that the suit was instituted on 21st April, 2003 against Homeland Footwear Ltd. and the Register, Joint Stock Companies. It was instituted after removal of the appellants from the Board on 13th July, 2002. It was also stated that this company was liquidated on 21st July, 2002 by an order of the Company Court.

47. Admittedly, Bangladesh Bank was not made party in the suit although it served show cause notices upon the appellants two years prior to the date of institution of the suit. The appellants had knowledge about the initiation of the proceedings by the Bangladesh Bank for their removal for suppression of material facts. Therefore, the passing of the decree will not stand in the way in taking any decision by the Bangladesh Bank since it has not been made party in the suit. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submitted that this decree is a collusive one which was obtained within one month of its institution on 25th March, 2003 without impleading the Bangladesh Bank and the Official Liquidator, and as such, the suit is also barred by section 250 of the Companies Act. It is not disputed by the appellants counsel that an order of winding up of the company was made on 21st July, 2002 and an Official Liquidator was also appointed before the institution of the suit.

48. Section 250 provides that "when a winding up order has been made or a provisional liquidator has been appointed, no suit or other legal proceedings shall be proceeded with or commenced against the company except by leave of the Court and subject to the terms as the court may impose". The policy underlying this provision is to protect the assets for equitable distribution among those entitled, and to prevent the administration being embarrassed by a general scramble of creditors. When a winding up order of a company has been made, the combined effect of this section, and sections 322 and 328 is that such order operates automatically as a stay of all actions, executions, distresses etc. against the company subject to the discretion of the Court to allow such actions to proceed notwithstanding the winding up. This section prevents the commencement of any other proceedings against the company after the appointment of the Official Liquidator without leave of the winding-up Court. There is no gainsaying the fact that the appellants by concealing the 'fact of winding-up order obtained a collusive decree which has no force of law and binding effect. The fact that even after removal of the appellants from the Board, he institution of the suit without impleading the Bangladesh Bank and the Official Liquidator, and impleading Homeland Footwear Ltd. as defendant and obtaining a decree within one month from the day its institution of the suit itself proved that it was a collusive decree.

49. Mr. Mahmud contended that the reasons based upon which the orders of removal were made were not relevant for making such orders, inasmuch as, the appellants were not defaulters within the meaning of section 5(Ga, Ga) of the Act of 1991. In this connection Mr Mahmud drew our attention to the inspection report submitted by Mr Md Rafiqul Islam at page 181, relevant at page 183 of the paper book. It was pointed out that the appellant Kamal Uddin Ahmed became share holder of the Homeland Footwear Ltd. by way of transfer of 25,000 (twenty five thousand) shares by Mrs. Taslima Akter and Ms. Salina Alam became a shareholder by transfer of 25,000 shares by her mother Mrs. Johora Alam. According to Mr. Mahmud, the combined shares held by Kamal Uddin and Salina Alam being less than 25% of the total shares, these two appellants could not be said to be defaulters within the meaning of the Act of 2001.

50. The transfer of shares revealed in the inspection report dated 25th January, 1998. The show cause notices were issued upon them on 8th October, 2001 after three years and nine months of submission of the report. Section 5(Ga-Ga) was inserted by way of amendment by Act XXIII of 2001 which came into effect on 16th April, 2001, Appellants did not state in the writ petition or in their replies to the show cause notices or in their concise statement that they held less than 25% of the total shares in Homeland Footwear Ltd. on the day of issuance of show cause notices, and therefore, they were not defaulters within the meaning of section 5(Ga-Ga) of the Act of 2001. What's more, these transfer of shares were made among the members of the same family in respect of a private limited company. There is allegation that the appellants maintained secrecy in changing the hands of shares and concealed the fact.

51. It is seen in a number of cases, the private companies are treating the same as a partnership business. Such companies make provision in the articles for transfer of shares to particular persons at a particular price. They are not void as being repugnant to absolute ownership or as standin4 to perpetuity. In articles of association of a private company provisions are sometimes made to the effect that any member desiring to sell any of his shares must notify the Board of the number of shares, the price and the name of the proposed transferee, and the Board must offer to the other share-holders the number of share, offered at the price and if the offer is accepted, the shares shall be transferred to the purchasers, if the shares are not accepted, the holder may sell them to third parties. The appellants did not produce the share register of the company or any other evidence showing that they held less amount of shares than the required members, for which, they were not defaulters within the amended provisions of law.

52. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, added that as the copy of the inquiry report was not supplied to the appellants the appellants were deprived of their right to take proper defence against the charges. In support of the contention reliance was given to the cases of Managing Director, ECIL vs B. Karunakar, (1993) 4 SCC 727, KI Shepherd vs Union of India, AIR 1998(686) and H.L. Trehan vs Union of India, AIR 1989 SC 568. These decisions have been cited on behalf of the respondents as well. I do not find any substance in the contention of Mr. Huq, inasmuch as, neither in the replies to the show cause notices nor in the petition of appeals the appellants stated that because of non-supply of the inquiry report they could not properly defend the charges brought against them. There is no statement at all in that regard. Only allegation they made was that they were not given personal hearing.

53. In the case of Shephard, the question was whether post decisional hearing satisfied the rules of natural justice. In the facts of the case it was held that they i.e. the writ petitioners have already been thrown out of employment and having been deprived of livelihood there is no justification to throw them out of employment and then to give them an opportunity of representation when the requirement is that they should be given an opportunity of being heard as a condition precedent to action and that once a decision has been taken, there is a tendency to uphold it and a representation may not yield any fruitful purpose.

54. In the case of HL Trehan, the similar views were taken. In that case two undertakings were vested in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd., which became a Government company. The chairman of the company issued a circular stating that consequence of taking over of a company, the question of rationalisation of the prerequisites admissible to the management staff in the manner stated in the circular. This circular was challenged by some employees on the ground that the terms and conditions of their service had been substantially altered. Admittedly the employees were not given opportunity of hearing before the circular was issued. In the context of the matter, it was argued that the authority who embarks upon a post-decisional hearing will naturally proceed with a close mind and there is hardly any chance of getting proper consideration of the representation, and as such, the post-decisional opportunity of hearing does not sub-serve the rules of natural justice and that the authority who embarks upon a post-decisional hearing will naturally proceed with closed mind and there is hardly any chance of getting a proper consideration of the representation at such post-decisional opportunity.

55. In B Karunakor's case, the question of law involved is whether the report of the inquiry officer who was appointed by the disciplinary authority to inquire into the charges against delinquent employee, is required to furnish inquiry report to the employee to enable him to make proper representation to the disciplinary authority before such authority arrives at its own finding with regard to the guilt. The Supreme Court noticed Article 311(2) of the constitution which provided "(2) No such person as aforesaid shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank except after an enquiry in which he has been informed of the charges against him and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges" and all previous decisions particularly the case Union of India vs Mohd. Ranzan Khan, (1991) 1 SCC 588 on the issue of service of inquiry report to the delinquent employee. It was also noticed that different Benches of the Central Administrative Tribunal, the High Courts and the Supreme Court took different views on the point.

56. This needed the Supreme Court to settle the law as the authorities all over the country had proceeded on the basis that there was no need to furnish a copy of the inquiry report and innumerable employees have been punished without giving them copies of the reports in some cases the orders of punishment have long since became final while other cases are pending in Courts in many cases, misconduct has been grave. The Supreme Court was of the view 'that the views taken in Mohd. Ramzan Khan (1991) 1 SCC 588) that the delinquent employee is entitled to the copy of the inquiry report before the disciplinary authority takes its decision is correct statement of law. On the basis of the charges levelled against him, the views taken in Mohd. Ramzan Khan should be followed and directed all appeals and special leave petitions be placed before an appropriate Bench with specific observations that the denial on the part of the authority in earlier cases to furnish the reports would be treated as no more than a technical mistake. This view was taken on the reasonings that "To reopen all disciplinary proceedings now would result in grave prejudice to administration which will far out-weigh the benefit of the employees concerned. Both Administrative reality and public interests do not, therefore, require that the orders of punishment passed prior to the decision in Mohd. Ramzan Khan case without furnishing report of the enquiry officer should be disturbed and the disciplinary proceedings which gave rise to the said order should be reopened on that account."

57. These are settled principles being followed by the superior courts over half a century and this Division also held in a number of cases that a delinquent employee should be supplied with the enquiry report before taking penal action against him and if there is violation it would offend the principle of natural justice. The facts of the reported cases are quite distinguishable from the facts of the present cases. These decisions will not help the appellants.

<u>58. The concept of procedural fairness has gained recognition in our statutes and the Constitution as well. Articles 27, 29, 31, 32, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, and 42 are those provisions which guaranteed due process rule. The rules of natural justice can operate only in areas not covered by any law validly made where a statute does not in terms exclude this rule or prior hearing. Thus this principle cannot be put into straight-jacket and its application would depend upon the particular facts and the circumstances of a situation. Thus, it is sometimes said 'natural justice is not capable of static and precise definition. It will also have been noted that the terms of the statutes conferring functions vary considerably, and range from the provision which confers a bare authority without giving any instruction as to how the function is to be carried out, through a wide variety of provisions in which deferent procedural formulas are prescribed, sometimes embodying one or more, to the exclusion of other requirements of justice, right up to those enactments which provide for a complete and comprehensive code of procedure embodying all the judicial rules and principles or fair play, which are necessary for the protection of the citizen.</u>

59. It is thus clear that the legislature may adopt principles of natural justice in their entirety and make them statutory for the purpose of implementation of a particular Act or may modify them for the purposes of another Act or may exclude them altogether for the purpose of another Act. The principles of natural justice or the fair play rule cannot override the statute law. The Courts must observe the provisions of statutes which direct a procedure inconsistent with the principles of justice recognised by the common law of England. Each Act must be examined and its terms interpreted to ascertain which course has been adopted in any particular case.

<u>60. Right to a hearing or representation before a decision affecting right of a person is embodied in the due process law understood in the sense the term has been used in the constitutional jargon. There is an express provision in the Act of 1991 which requires that the andialteram partem rule should be followed before removal of a person from the Board. If the statute makes itself clear on the point then no more questions arises to decide otherwise. When the statute is silent, the law in a given case make an implication and apply the principle. The requirement of law for taking action under section 46 (1) of the Act of 2001 is that “ তাহাকে উহার বিরুদ্ধে কারন প্রদর্শনের জন্য যুক্তিসংগত সুযোগ দিতে হইবে” that is, the person against whom the order is to be made shall be given a reasonable opportunity for explanation against the proposed order. The fairness in action as per law demands that an opportunity to present an explanation should be given to the person affected. Fair play in action required that an opportunity should be given to the removed members of the Board to see and reply to the charges before reaching to the conclusion that there is a 'prima-facie' or 'reasonable' case against them. They cannot claim anything more than that.</u>

61. If the principle of personal hearing is extended whenever statutory authorities are vested with the power to exercise discretion in contravention with statutory provisions, it shall lead to chaotic conditions. Many statutory authorities which are empowered to perform quasi judicially are expected to apply their judicial mind over the grievances of the aggrieved persons but it cannot be held that before dismissing their claims in all events the quasi-judicial authorities must hear the aggrieved persons. When principles of natural justice require an opportunity to be heard before an adverse order is made, it does not in all circumstances mean a personal hearing. The requirement is to be complied with by affording him an opportunity to present his case before such quasi-judicial authority which is expected to apply his judicial mind to the issues involved. If the statute provides for a provision for personal hearing he has no choice other than that of giving such personal hearing.

<u>62. The statute does require the rule of prior opportunity and that opportunity was afforded to the appellant but it does not provide for a personal hearing apart from the opportunity provided in it. The appellants also did not claim such hearing before the orders of removal were made. Though the statute did not provide for post-decisional hearing, they were given such hearing as they desired for such hearing at the appellate stage. Section 48(2) authorised the Board of Directors of Bangladesh Bank to hear an appeal from an order made by the Governor of the Bank and their 'decision shall be final." Therefore, the Board of Directors have been given full powers to sit on appeal from the order or decision of the Governor. The statutory provisions for an administrative appeal on merits are sufficient to negative the existence of any implied duty to hear in person before the original decision was made.</u>

<u>63. Wade in his Administrative Law, Fifth Edition, at page 34 said, the system of judicial review is radically deferent from the system of appeals. When hearing an appeal the Court is concerned with the merits of the decision under appeal. When subjecting some administrative act or order to judicial review, the Court is concerned with its legality. On an appeal the question is bright or wrong? Rights of appeal are always statutory. Judicial review, on the other hand, is the exercise of the Court's inherent power to determine whether action is lawful or not and to award suitable relief. Where the proceeding is an appeal, some superior Court or authority will reconsider the decision of some lower Court or authority on its merit. There are also many statutory rights of appeal, as in the present case, from one administrative authority to another. The provision of appeal provided before the Board of Directors was truly a rehearing, and the appellants had a fair and adequate opportunity of dealing with any findings which were critical to them in the Governor's orders.</u>

<u>64. Even if it is assumed that there was unfairness by reason of not giving a personal-hearing was cured by the process of the appeal. Dillon, L.J in MacMahon in the context of the arguments of Lord Wilberforce in Calvin vs Carr (1980) AC 574 and per Barwick, CJ in Twist vs Randwick Munical Council (1976) 12 ALR 379, 384 stated 'If the scope of any permissible appeal is limited, so that it does not involve an examination of the circumstances of the case de novo on evidence not limited to that which was before the original tribunal, it may well be that the appellate hearing will not cure the defects of the original decision.' The opinion of Lord Dillon was that 'failure was fully cured by the hearing in the Divisional Court under the statutory appeal process'. The power of the Board of Directors, as observed above, was not limited but on merits, and the appellate authority had the power to reconsider and reevaluate the decision of the Governor of the Bangladesh Bank. It involved a re-examination of the circumstances of the cases de-novo on the materials which were placed before the Governor. The principle of audi alteram partem, as observed above, cannot be imprisoned in the straight-jacket of a cast-iron formula and this rule can operate only in areas not covered by any law. Where a statute conferring the power, is silent with regard to a pre-decisional hearing to the affected person a post decisional hearing would cure the defect. To make the point clear, a post-decisional hearing can obliterate the procedural deficiency of a pre-decisional hearing. There is thus, no violation of the principle of natural justice or breach of the principles of fairness. I find no reason to depart from the statements of law argued by the House of Lords, Supreme Courts of Canada and India.</u>

65. Accordingly, I would dismiss the appeals but without making any order as to costs.

Nazmun Ara Sultana J: Since all these four civil appeals by leave have arisen out of a common judgment and order dated 16-3-2003 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.  3285 of 2003, 3286 of 2003, 3287 of 2003 and 3288 of 2003 these have been heard together and are being disposed of by this single judgment.

68. The appellants filed the above writ petitions challenging the rejection of their appeals under section 48 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. The case of all the four writ petitioners was same which, in short, was as follows :—

69. The writ petitioners were members of the Board of Directors of Social Investment Bank Limited (respondent No. 4) since 1995 until they were unlawfully removed from the directorship of the said bank.
