70. The writ petitioners preferred appeals before the respondent No.  3 against the order of their removal from the directorship of the respondent No.  4 Bank as per section 48 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. They also wrote letter to the respondent Nos. 1 on 15th July, 2002 requesting him to keep their removal order in abeyance pending hearing of their appeals, but the said letter did not yield any result. Thereafter, the writ petitioners filed Writ Petition Nos.  3526-29 of 2002 challenging their removal orders from the Board of Directors of respondent No.  4 bank. While the said writ petitions were pending the writ petitioners were directed to appear before the respondent No.  3 for hearing of the appeals filed by them under section 48 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. The appeals were subsequently rejected upholding the petitioners removal order. Thereafter, the petitioners filed the Writ Petition Nos.  3285-3288 of 2003 challenging the rejection orders of their appeals and obtained rule. They of course, withdrew the Writ Petition Nos.  3526-29 of 2002 which they earlier filed challenging their removal order.

71. The further case of the writ petitioners was that they filed Title Suit No.  138 of 2003 against Homeland Footwear Limited seeking a decree declaring that the plaintiffs were not the directors of the defendant No.  1 company and that the returns (Form-IX) purportedly submitted by the company with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies were illegal and without compliance of the provisions of the Companies Act, 1994 and also a decree of mandatory injunction against the proforma defendant No. 2, Registrar of Joint Stock Companies directing him to amend the records of Homeland Footwear Limited deleting the names of the petitioners from the list of directors. In that suit, on the prayer of the plaintiffs, the court issued an ad-interim order of injunction on 21-4-2003 directing the defendants to treat declaration of the company made in Form-IX as inoperative till the next fixed date. That suit also was ultimately decreed. That the rejection of appeals of the writ petitioners as such has been without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. That the writ petitioners were not given any opportunity of hearing before their removal from the directorship of the Bank. That there had never been any allegation against the writ petitioners of influencing the respondent No. 4 Bank in not inserting the information of taking loan by the defaulter company from respondent No. 4 Bank in the statement submitted by respondent No. 4 Bank to Bangladesh Bank or in not impleading the writ petitioners as defendants in the suit filed by respondent No. 4 Bank against the defaulter company for recovery of loan or in not invoking section 17 of the Act-as alleged in the removal order and no show cause notice was issued upon the writ petitioners regarding these allegations. That the removal of the writ petitioners from the Board of Directors of the respondent No. 4 Bank and also the rejection of their appeals have been illegal and, as such, are liable to be set-aside.

72. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in one set and respondent Nos. 5 to 9 in another set con-tested the rules by filing affidavits-in-opposition. The material case of these contesting respondents was that the writ petitioners while were members of Board of directors of respondent No. 4 Social Investment Bank Ltd. were also directors of the loan defaulter company Homeland Footwear Limited in contravention of provisions of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 and concealed that fact from respondent No. 4 Bank that Bangladesh Bank constituted a high powered committee to enquire into this allegation against the writ petitioners and this enquiry committee, on thorough enquiry, found the allegation proved. That the writ petitioners were removed from the Board of Directors of the Social Investment Bank Limited after compliance of all requirements of law; that the rejection of the appeals of the writ petitioners against their removal order also was most lawful and justified; that the competent authority, after giving proper opportunity of hearing to the writ petitioners and considering all other materials rejected the appeals of the writ petitioners rightly; that there has been no illegality in passing the removal order and also the impugned rejection orders of the appeals filed by the writ petitioners against their removal order.

73. The contesting respondents challenged also the legality and validity of the decree of Title Suit No. 138 of 2003 as mentioned in the writ petitions contending inter-alia, that this suit was collusive and the decree passed therein also is collusive and fraudulent that the writ petitioners in collusion with some officials of Homeland Footwear Limited Company managed that decree. That the Homeland Footwear Limited Company was wound up by an order of Company Bench of the High Court Division on 21-7-2002 and that order was upheld by the Appellate Division on 14-1-2003 and a liquidator also was appointed for that company. But the Title Suit No.  138 of 2003 was filed after winding up order, so it was barred under section 250 of the Companies Act, as neither sanction of the Court was obtained for filing that suit nor the liquidator was made a party in that suit and for this reason also the decree passed in title suit No.  138 of 2003 is a nullity.

74. The High Court Division on hearing the learned Counsel of all the parties and on consideration of the facts and circumstances, discharged the rules in all the four writ petitions holding that there were sufficient materials before the authority concerned to prove that the writ petitioners were directors of the defaulter company Homeland Footwear Limited and that the authority concerned rightly removed the petitioners from the directorship of the Social Investment Bank Limited on compliance of all requirements of law and, as such, the rejection of the appeals filed by the writ petitioners under section 48 of the Bank Companies Act 1991 against their removal order also was justified and lawful.

75. Being aggrieved by this judgment and order of the High Court Division the four writ petitioners filed four Civil Petitions for leave to appeal Nos.  703 to 706 of 2003 seeking leave to appeal and leave was granted to examine whether actions of Bangladesh Bank in removing the appellants from the Board of Directors of Social Investment Bank Limited were justified and in accordance with law.

76. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and the respondent Nos. 5 to 8 have appeared in these appeals and contested.

77. We have heard the learned Counsel of all the parties in details.

78. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Senior Counsel for the appellants has assailed the removal orders of the appellants and the impugned rejection orders of their appeals on the main ground of violation of principle of natural justice. Mr Mahmud has contended that in this case there has been gross violation of principle of natural justice in removing the appellants from the Board of Directors of Social Investment Bank Limited. The learned Counsel has identified three factors, viz., non-giving of personal hearing to the appellants, non-furnishing of reports of enquiry committee and standing committee to them and also adding of three new allegations in the removal order-which, according to him, have caused violation of principle of natural justice. The learned Counsel has argued that the appellants though gave reply to the show cause notices claiming personal hearing but they were not called upon for personal hearing and as a result the appellants were denied reasonable opportunity of defending themselves properly. Mr Mahmud has argued that it is now well settled by the decisions of the apex Courts of this country and also of other countries that before condemning any person he should be given a fair opportunity of being heard, even if, the relevant rules do not require so; that non-giving of personal heating to the appellants has denied the requirement of natural justice. Mr Mahmud has next argued that non-furnishing of the reports of enquiry committee and the standing committee also has deprived the appellants of the reasonable opportunity of defending themselves properly which, according to him, has denied the requirement of natural justice. The learned Counsel has argued that these reports were the basis of the allegations against the appellants and, as such, the appellants ought to have been supplied copy of these reports for making them enable to controvert the materials relied on for proving the allegations; that the non-supply of the copy of these reports also has deprived the appellants of their right to controvert these allegations brought against them. The learned Counsel for the appellants has then argued that the allegations on which the appellants were removed from the Board of Directors of the bank were not mentioned in the show cause notice and for this defect also the removal order has been illegal. Mr Mahmud has read out both the show cause notice dated 8-10-2001 the annexure-C and the removal order dated 13-7-2002 the annexure-I and has argued that in the removal order three new allegations were added which were not mentioned in the show cause notice and, as such, petitioners had no scope to deny or controvert these new allegations and thus gross violation of natural justice was caused. The learned Counsel for the appellants has argued that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the well-settled principle of natural justice that the allegations which constitute the basis for action proposed to be taken has to be mentioned in the show cause notice itself and that the non-mentioning of these allegations in the show cause notice made the removal order illegal. In support of his argument the learned Counsel for the appellants has cited several decisions reported in 48 DLR (AD) 20, (Bangladesh Telecom (Pvt.) Ltd. vs T & T Board), 1964 Appeal Cases 40, AIR 1988 (SC) 686, (KI Shephard vs Union of India), (1978) 1 All England Law Reports, 586 (H Sabey and Co. vs Secretary of State).

79. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud has made argument to the effect also that the appellants were not at all defaulter loanee as they all had total less then 6% share in the defaulter company Homeland Footwear Limited and, as such, they were not liable for being removed from the Board of Directors of the lending bank Social Investment Bank Limited.

80. Mr Rafique-ul Huq, the learned Senior Counsel has appeared for respondent No.  4 Social Investment Bank. Limited. Mr Huq also has advanced argument to effect that the removal of the appellants from the Board of Directors of Social Investment Bank Limited has been in gross violation of principles of natural justice and, as such, illegal. Mr Huq has argued that the appellants ought to have been supplied with the copy of the enquiry report which was the requirement of principal of natural justice; that non-supply of the enquiry report to the appellants is violation of natural justice and for this reason the removal order of the appellants cannot be sustained in law. In support of this argument the learned Counsel has submitted a photocopy of the judgment of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No.  5231 of 2005.

81. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate has appeared in all these four appeals for respondent Nos.  1 to 2. Controverting the arguments of the learned Counsel for the appellants and the respondent No.  4. Mr Islam has advanced argument to the effect that in this case there has been no violation of natural justice at all. That as per requirement of section 46 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 the appellants were served with show cause notices wherein the allegations against them were clearly mentioned and that the appellants also gave reply to those show cause notices denying elaborately the allegations against them. The learned Counsel has read out the reply of the appellants to the show cause notices the annexure-D and has pointed out that in this reply to show cause notice the appellants did not claim any personal hearing at all. The learned Counsel has argued the appellants, in fact, did not require any personal hearing as they gave elaborate reply to show cause notices denying all allegations; that if the appellants hold claimed personal hearing and were refused then only they could have argued the violation of natural justice.

82. Mr Islam has argued also that in this case there was no necessity of furnishing the copy of the reports of enquiry committee and standing committee to the appellants as the appellants were adequately apprised of the allegations brought against them and they also denied these allegations by elaborate written submission and that the appellants were not prejudiced at all for non-furnishing of these reports. Mr Islam has contended that giving of personal hearing or supply of enquiry reports are not the requirement for satisfying the principle of natural justice, that the requirement of natural justice is that the person against whom the proposed action is to be taken must get reasonable opportunity to defend himself properly. The learned Counsel for the respondent Nos.  1 to 2 has argued also that in this case the appellants were heard personally in the departmental appeals filed by them against their removal order and this personal hearing in the appellate stage has cured the defect, if any, caused in the pre-decisional stage. In support of this argument the learned Counsel has referred to some decisions reported in (1993) 4 Supreme Court Cases 727, (Managing Director, ECIL vs B Karunakar), (1989) Supp (2) SCC 462, (Carborundum Universal Ltd. vs CBDT), (2003)4 SCC 557, (1996) 4 SCC 69, (Union of India vs Jesus Sales Corporation), (1987) 1 All England Law Reports 1118, (Lloyd vs McMahon), (1979) 2 All England Law Reports 440 (Calvin vs Carr).

83. As regards the contention of adding some new allegations in the removal order the reply of the learned Counsel for the respondent Nos. 1 to 3 is that in fact these were no new allegations, rather these were the consequences of the allegations which were mentioned in the show cause notice and that the appellants were removed on the allegations mentioned in the show cause notice and not on these allegations mentioned in the removal order and, as such, the appellants were not prejudiced at all for mentioning these new allegations in the removal order.

84. As to the alleged decree of Title Suit No. 138 of 2003 Mr Islam has argued that this decree is a collusive and also invalid. The learned Counsel has stated that the defaulter company Homeland Footwear Limited was wound up by Company Bench of the High Court Division by order dated 21-7-2002 which was upheld by the Appellate Division on 10-1-2003, but the Title Suit No. 138 of 2003 was filed in April 2003 i.e. after winding up order of this company without any sanction of the Court and without impleading the liquidator appointed for the company and, as such, the decree passed in this suit is illegal. The learned Counsel has argued that the High Court Division considering all these facts, circumstances and materials rightly found that the decree in this Title Suit No.  138 of 2003 was collusive and, as such, cannot be taken into consideration at all. The learned Counsel has made submissions to the effect also that there were sufficient evidence to prove that the petitioners were directors of the defaulter company and they concealed this fact to the respondent No.  4 Social Investment Bank Limited and, as such, the High Court Division committed no wrong or illegality in discharging the rules.

85. Mr AKM Nazrul Islam, the learned Advocate has appeared for respondent Nos.  5 and 8 and Mr. Abdur Razzak, the learned Advocate has appeared for respondent No.  6. Both the learned Counsel while adopting the arguments made by Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for respondent Nos.  1 and 2 have cited several decisions in support of their contentions that the removal order of the appellants and also the rejection of their appeals have not been illegal or unlawful on any count.

86. We have considered the submissions of the learned Counsel of all the parties and gone through the impugned judgment of the High Court Division, the show cause notices-the annexure-C the reply of the petitioners to the show cause notice the annexure-D, the removal order of the petitioners the annexure-I, the impugned rejection order of the petitioners appeal the annexure-A and other necessary papers on record.

87. Before the High Court Division all the writ petitioners assailed their removal from the Board of Directors of Social Investment Bank Limited on the main ground that they were never members of Board of Directors of loan defaulter company Homeland Footwear Limited as they were never elected or consented to act as directors of the said defaulter company. However, the High Court Division, on consideration of submissions of the learned Counsel of both the sides, the materials on record and facts and circumstances, came to definite finding that there were sufficient materials before the authority concerned which proved the allegation that these petitioners were Directors of that defaulter company. This finding and decision of the High Court Division though has been assailed in the concise statements submitted in these appeals, but at the time of hearing of the appeals no forceful argument was made from the side of the appellants to controvert this finding of the High Court Division. Admittedly Bangladesh Bank formed an enquiry committee with high officials to enquire into this allegation of the petitioners being directors of the defaulter company and this enquiry committee, after thorough enquiry, found the allegation proved and submitted report stating amongst others that the petitioners subsequently resigned from the directorship of the defaulter Homeland Footwear Limited and that immediate after their resignation some close relations like wife and daughter of some of the appellants were appointed as directors of that defaulter company in their place and they also acted as such remaining present in some meetings of the Board of Directors of the company. This very fact that the wife and daughter of two of these appellants were appointed as directors of the said defaulter company just after resignation of these appellants and they also acted as directors of that company has not been denied at all by these appellants either before the High Court Division or before this court. The High Court Division in its impugned judgment has clearly mentioned this fact also while discussing other materials on record in support of directorship of the appellants in the defaulter company. But in spite of that the appellants did not deny this very fact before this Division. In fact the learned Counsel for the appellants did not make any strong submissions on the finding of the High Court Division to the effect that there were sufficient materials before the authority concerned to prove that the writ petitioners were directors of the defaulter company.

88. In these appeals it has been pleaded that a competent court has already declared that these appellants were not directors of the defaulter company Homeland Footwear Limited and, as such, the removal of the appellants from the directorship of Social Investment Bank Limited on the ground that they were directors of that defaulter company has been illegal and unlawful. But it appears that this plea also of the appellants was duly considered by the High Court Division. The High Court Division, on discussing the facts, circumstances and materials on record, clearly held that this alleged decree passed in Title Suit No.  138 of 2003 declaring that the writ petitioners were not directors of the defaulter company was collusive and, as such, cannot be taken into consideration at all. Before this Division it has further been submitted from the side of the con-testing respondents that this defaulter company Homeland Footwear Limited was wound by the Company Bench of the High Court Division by the order dated 21-7-2002 and this order was upheld by the Appellate Division on 10-1-2003, but the alleged Title Suit No.  138 of 2003 was filed in April 2003 i.e. after winding up order of this company without any sanction of the court and without impleading the liquidator appointed for this defaulter company. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for the contesting respondent Nos.  1-2 has pointed out these facts before this Division and has argued that the decree of Title Suit No.  138 of 2003 has been illegal and invalid for these reasons also. We find no reason not to accept this argument of the learned Counsel for the respondent Nos.  1-3. Since before filing of Title Suit No.  138 of 2003 the defaulter company was wound up by the order of the court and since a liquidator also was appointed for this defaulter company this suit filed without sanction of the court in contravention of section 250 of the Companies Act, 1994 and without impleading the liquidator as a party was illegal and for this reason the decree passed in that suit is illegal and invalid. So the High Court Division did not commit any wrong in holding that the decree of Title Suit No.  138 of 2003 as alleged by the writ petitioners cannot be taken into consideration at all. It should be mentioned here that before this Division the learned Counsel for the appellants did not make any submission to the effect that the decree of Title Suit No.  138 of 2003 is lawful and, as such, so long this decree stands the appellants cannot be said to be directors of the defaulter company Homeland Footwear Limited.

89. Before this Appellate Division the ground which has been pressed with much force is that the requirement of natural justice were not met in removing the appellants from the directorship of Social Investment Bank Limited and, as such, the removal orders have been illegal. It has been contended from the side of the appellants that the non-giving of personal hearing and non-furnishing of reports of enquiry committee and standing committee to the appellants deprived them of the reason-able opportunity of defending themselves properly and thus caused violation of natural justice.

<u>90. We have considered this contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants deeply. The rule of reasonable opportunity and the principle of natural justice have been evolved by the pronouncements of the courts. These are not any statutory rules. Under different situations and conditions the requirement of compliance of the principle of natural justice vary. Natural justice generally requires that the persons against whom the proposed punitive action is to be taken be given reasonable opportunity to defend themselves. Rule of audi alteram partem requires that before a person is punished an opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment should be afforded to him. Furnishing of enquiry report and giving of personal hearing may not always be requirement of natural justice. Where the delinquent is served with show cause notice stating clearly the allegations against him and the delinquent be able to give effective reply denying all those allegations and the non-furnishing of the enquiry report or non-giving of personal hearing do not prejudice the delinquent the allegation of violation of natural justice should not be entertained. The court cannot insist that under all circumstances and under different statutory provisions the delinquent has to be furnished the enquiry report and given personal hearing.</u>

91. In the present case we are to see whether the appellants were prejudiced by non-furnishing of enquiry reports and non-giving of personal hearing.

92. Admittedly the appellants were served with show cause notice the annexure-C wherein the allegations brought against them were clearly stated. In this show cause notice it was clearly alleged that while the appellants were members of Board of Directors of the Social Investment Bank Limited they became the directors of loan defaulter company namely M/s Homeland Footwear Limited and acted as such from 13-3-1997 to 24-2-1998 and that the appellants concealed this fact from the Social Investment Bank Limited and subsequently they resigned from the directorship of that defaulter company without taking consent from the lending bank-Social Investment Bank Limited as per requirement of section 27 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. In the show cause notice it was also clearly stated that the connection of the appellants with the loan defaulter company and also the concealment of that fact from Social Investment Bank Limited was detrimental to the interest of the depositors of the said bank and also against public interest. These show cause notices adequately apprised the appellants of the allegations brought against them and the appellants also gave effective reply to these show cause notices denying all these allegations elaborately. It should be mentioned here that Bangladesh Bank constituted an enquiry committee with its high officials to enquire into the allegations against the appellants. This enquiry committee, after through enquiry, submitted a report with the opinion that the allegation against the appellants were found proved. This enquiry report of the enquiry committee was scrutinized and considered by standing committee formed by Bangladesh Bank as per section 46 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. The standing committee, on consideration of this enquiry report submit-ted a report and on the basis of this report of the standing committee the appellants were removed from the directorship of the Social Investment Bank Limited. However, it appears that the allegations against the appellants were proved from the official documents including the statement (Form No.  IX) submitted by the defaulter company Homeland Footwear Limited to the Registrar of the Joint Stock Company. In this statement the names of all the appellants were mentioned as directors. From the record it appears that the appellants were well informed about this statement in Form No.  IX submitted to the Registrar of the Joint Stock Company and they, before the High Court Division, alleged that the previous Managing Director of the defaulter company might have included their names in that statement in Form No.  IX and created all other papers with an ulterior motive. So it appears that the evidence and materials which were based in the enquiry report for finding the allegations against the appellants proved came to the knowledge of the appellants and the appellants also got opportunity to controvert those materials and evidence in the reply to show cause notices and also during hearing of the appeal by appearing personally and making statement before the appellate authority. So it appears that the non-supply of the reports of the enquiry committee and the standing committee did not prejudice the appellants at all. We, therefore, cannot accept the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellants that the non-supply of the copies of the reports of the enquiry committee and the standing committee deprived the appellants of the opportunity of defending themselves properly and thereby the requirement of natural justice was denied.

93. In their reply to show cause notice the appellants though have elaborately denied the allegations against them as stated in the show cause notice but did not claim any personal hearing. In the last para, i.e. para No.  13 of this reply the appellants have stated only thus: "should you need any clarification or further assistance in resolving the issue, our client is ready to extend all cooperation and would not hesitate to attend any hearing." This very quoted sentence of the reply of the appellants to show cause notice proves that the appellants actually did not claim any personal hearing, rather they expressed only that if the authority required they would attend personal hearing. So the appellants contention that they were refused personal hearing in spite of their claim is not acceptable at all. The appellants were given opportunity to make written representation as regards the allegations made against them and they also submitted elaborate written representation denying all those allegations and the authority concerned considered those written representations of the appellants in passing the orders of their removal. In the circumstances we do not find that the appellants were prejudiced for non-giving of personal hearing. In this connection we may refer a decision of Indian Supreme Court in the case of Carborundum Universal Ltd. vs CBDT reported in 1989 Supp (2) SCC 462 reported in (1989 Supp (2) SCC 462 cited by the learned Advocate for the contesting respondents. In that case it was held:—

<u>"Personal hearing in every situation is not necessary and there can be compliance of the requirement of hearing when a right to represent is given and the decision is made on a consideration thereof."</u>

<u>94. However, it appears that all these Appellants were given personal hearing in the departmental appeals filed by them against the order of their removal. In these appeals the appellate authority took personal hearing of all the appellants and considered their submissions in disposing of these appeals. The appeals are continuation of the proceeding. So it appears that during continuation of the proceeding all the appellants were given personal hearing. The impugned rejection order of the appeals-the annexure-A shows that the appellate authority considered the statements of the appellants which they made in their personal hearing. The personal hearing of the appellants in the appellate stage cured the defect, if any, of non-giving of personal hearing in pre-decisional stage. Their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Canara Bank and others vs Debasis Das reported in (2003) 4 SCC 557 expressed this view. They held that where in absence of pre-decisional hearing opportunity of post-decisional "hearing was granted by the appellate authority by giving personal hearing to the employee and no prejudice had been shown there was no violation of principle of natural justice.</u>

95. In the present case the appellants got adequate opportunity to defend themselves denying the allegations brought against them by submitting written representations and by making personal hearing before the appellate authority and the appellate authority also duly considered both their written representations and oral submissions. So the appellants were not at all prejudiced for non-giving of personal hearing at pre-decisional stage and, as such, there was no violation of principle of natural justice.

96. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Counsel for the appellants has cited some decisions in support of his contention that non-furnishing of the enquiry reports and non-giving of personal hearing to the delinquent amounts to violation of natural justice. Mr Rafique-ul Huq, the learned Counsel for respondent No.  4 Social Investment Bank Limited also has filed a photocopy of the judgment passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.  5251 of 2005 in support of his contention that non-furnishing of the enquiry reports to the delinquent makes the punitive action taken against him illegal. We have gone through all these decisions cited by the learned Counsel for the appellants and respondent No. 4. It appears that in all these cited cases the delinquents were found to have been prejudiced gravely for non-furnishing of the enquiry report and non-giving of personal hearing. So, evidently, these cited decisions are not applicable in this present case. In this case we have found that non-furnishing of the enquiry reports and non-giving of personal hearing to the appellants at pre-decisional stage did not prejudice them at all and, as such, there was no violation of natural justice.

97. The next contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants is that the removal orders of the appellants show that they were removed on some other allegations which were not mentioned in the show cause notice. We have examined both the show cause notice dated 8-10-2001 the annexure-C and the removal order dated 13-7-2002 the annexure-I. In this removal order it has been stated that the standing committee formed as per section 48 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 examined the reply of the appellants to show cause notice dated 8-10-2001 and it was revealed therefrom that the appellants influenced the Social Investment Bank Limited (i) not to include the information regarding taking of loan by defaulter company from the Social Investment Bank Limited in the statements submitted by it to Bangladesh Bank, (ii) not to make the appellants party in the suit filed by the Social Investment Bank Limited against the defaulter company for realization of outstanding loan and (iii) not to invoke section 17 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 against the appellants. But this removal order does not at all tell that the appellants were removed for these three reasons as stated above. Rather, from reading of this removal order it becomes very much clear that the appellants were removed from the Board of Directors of the Social Investment Bank Limited on the allegations which were mentioned in the show cause notices. The above stated three other allegations as mentioned in the removal order are the consequences of the main allegations mentioned in the show cause notices and these were revealed from the own reply of the appellants to the show cause notices. However, from this removal order it does not appear at all that the appellants were removed on these three allegations mentioned in this removal order.

98. The decision in the case of Bangladesh Telecom (Pvt.) Ltd. vs T and T Board reported in 48 DLR (AD) 20 cited by the learned Counsel for the appellants thus, evidently, is of no help for the appellants of this case. In that cited case it was held that the facts which constitute the valid basis of cancellation of the license have to be alleged in the show cause notice itself. In the present case the facts which were stated in the show cause notice are the basis of removal of the appellants.

99. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud has made some argument to the effect also that the appellants themselves are not loan defaulter as defined in section 5(ga ga) of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 as the total share of all the appellants in the defaulter company is less then 6%. We do not understand why the learned Counsel has advanced this argument. In this case the appellants were removed from the directorship of the Social Investment Bank Limited for the reasons that they were directors of a defaulter company which took loan from this Social Investment Bank Limited and concealed this fact from this bank. This act of the appellants was considered by Bangladesh Bank detrimental to the interest of the depositors of the bank and also against public interest and, as such, Bangladesh Bank removed the appellants from the directorship of the Social Investment Bank Limited as per section 46 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. So whether the appellants themselves were defaulter or not that is not material at all to be considered in these appeals.

100. However, in view of above discussion it is evident that the High Court Division rightly discharged the rules holding rightly that the removal of the appellants from the Board of Directors of the Social Investment Bank Limited and also the rejection of their appeals filed against that removal orders were lawful being made quite in accordance with law. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, therefore, calls for no interference.

101. In the circumstances all these four appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs.
